title: Ignorance — mistaking the passing for the permanent (2.4–2.5)
hook: Patanjali defines the root of every affliction as four simple mix-ups, and the first is mistaking the passing for the permanent

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five afflictions, the kleshas, avidya first. Ignorance, I-ness, attraction, aversion, clinging. Did you trace a reaction to its root? Today, the root under all the roots. Day four hundred forty-nine.

You buy a new phone and, for a week, it feels like it will make you happy forever. You get a compliment and replay it for days, as if it settled who you are. You lose an argument and feel, for a whole afternoon, like that's the permanent truth about you. None of these were lies, exactly. They were mix-ups. Something passing got treated as something lasting. Patanjali puts that kind of mix-up at the very bottom of human trouble.
screen: `A NEW PHONE: HAPPY FOREVER.` → `A COMPLIMENT: WHO I AM.` → `THE PASSING, TAKEN AS LASTING.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.4: ignorance is the field for the others, whether they are dormant, thin, interrupted or fully active. Field, kshetra, like soil. I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging all grow out of it. And they can be in four states. Dormant, asleep like seeds in winter. Thin, weakened by practice. Interrupted, pushed down for a while by a stronger feeling. Or active, in full bloom. Then sutra 2.5 defines avidya with four mix-ups. Taking the impermanent as permanent. Taking the impure as pure. Taking what brings pain as pleasant. And taking what is not the self as the self. Notice that avidya isn't an empty space where knowledge should be. Vidya means knowledge; a-vidya is its opposite, an active wrong knowing that feels completely true from the inside. The commentator Vyasa compares it to how an enemy isn't merely the absence of a friend; it's the opposite of one. And the last mix-up is the deepest: taking the body, the mind, the moods, the roles, as the self, when in Patanjali's system the self is the seer, the one who watches them. You've already practiced the remedy, in chapter one: the seer resting in itself. Here's the same truth from the other side. The trouble begins the moment the seer seems to become what it sees.
screen: `THE FIELD THE OTHERS GROW IN.` · `DORMANT, THIN, INTERRUPTED, ACTIVE.` · `FOUR MIX-UPS.` · then, large: `NOT-SELF TAKEN AS SELF.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Notice something in you that feels permanent right now: a mood, a worry, a sense of who you are today. Hold it lightly, and ask: has this always been here? Will it always be? Watch it for a few breaths, and see whether it shifts, even a little. Then notice what has been watching it the whole time, the part that saw the mood come and will see it go. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Ignorance. Avidya: not a lack of facts but a wrong knowing, taking the passing for the permanent, the painful for the pleasant, the not-self for the self.
Your line: avidya. When something today feels like forever, a mood, a win, a loss, whisper to yourself: passing. And watch what changes. Day four hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: In yoga and Vedanta teaching, avidya is treated as the root problem, and students practice discernment, noticing what passes and what remains, as the way to loosen it.

myth: avidya means simply not knowing something
it's a wrong knowing, the opposite of knowledge, not just its absence.
Patanjali calls ignorance the field for the other afflictions
sutra 2.4: the soil the others grow in.
afflictions can be dormant, thin, interrupted or active

fork.setup: a bad day makes you feel you'll always be like this. which mix-up of 2.5 is at work?
fork.reveal: the first mix-up in 2.5: the passing taken for the lasting. moods, wins and losses all pass.

original.note: Sanskrit avidyā: ignorance, wrong knowing; a- (not) + vidyā (knowledge). the field for the other afflictions.

trapdoor: what you thought: ignorance means not knowing.
what it means: a wrong knowing: the passing taken as permanent, the not-self taken as the self.

what a scholar hears: Vyasa argues the a- in avidya marks an opposite, not an absence, as an enemy (amitra) is not merely no friend; 2.4 lists four states of the kleshas: prasupta, tanu, vichchhinna, udara.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 2.4 (ignorance as the field; four states)
Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 2.5 (the four mix-ups)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 2.5 (avidya as an opposite, like amitra)

notes: Vyasa's amitra (enemy, not merely absence of a friend) analogy on 2.5: confirm.
'Impure as pure' (ashuchi as shuchi): Vyasa's example concerns the body; left general.
